newsitem.title: JAPAN: FORECAST - Japan Jan-March GDP to show strong growth.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Japan Jan-March GDP to show strong growth.

text.p: Japan's economy is expected to have posted strong growth in the January-March quarter, boosted by a jump in consumer spending ahead of the rise in the sales tax in April, but economists say the tempo will slow as the tax measure begins to bite.

"Spending ahead of the tax hike was very strong. Private consumption was the main force behind growth," said Yoshito Sakakibara, vice president of economic and market analysis at Salomon Brothers Asia.
"But (strong consumption) will not last," he added.
Japan raised its national consumption tax to five percent from three percent on April 1, and the move was preceded by a rush of consumer buying.

The Economic Planning Agency is expected to announce gross domestic product (GDP) data for the January-March period either next week or the week after. It will flag the timing of the announcement 48 hours in advance.

Economists polled by Reuters said on average they expect real GDP for the period to have grown 1.1 percent from the previous quarter, which registered a growth rate of 1.0 percent. Forecasts ranged from 0.3 percent to 1.6 percent growth.
On an annualised basis, the average of economists' forecasts was 4.3 percent growth.
They said that, along with private consumption, corporate capital spending was the driving force behind growth in the first quarter of calender 1997.

Most economists forecast private consumption to have grown by more than two percent from the previous quarter, while capital spending was expected to show a quarter-on-quarter rise for the ninth consecutive quarter.
In contrast, a slump in housing investment and public works spending is expected to have weighed on overall growth during the period.
Housing investment is likely to have fallen from the prior quarter as demand ahead of the pending tax increase had already been waning since last autumn, economists said.

Net exports, which supported growth in the prior two quarters, are unlikely to have contributed to growth in the January-March period as tax-related domestic demand led to an increase in imports, economists said.

Although Japan's exports continued to show solid gains on a year-on-year basis, backed by a weak yen, the rise in imports will have offset this growth in the first quarter, said Susumu Kato, chief economist at BZW Securities (Japan).

Economists said that, as a result of strong January-March growth, the Japanese economy will have achieved the government's target of 2.5 percent GDP growth for fiscal year 1996/97, ended March 31. According to EPA data, the target would be reached even with a 0.63 percent decline in GDP during the period.
But economists said the government's target of 1.9 percent growth for the current fiscal year would be a more difficult hurdle, considering the expected impact of the tax rise.
"Fiscal consolidation measures will lead to negative growth in public works and will also suppress private consumption," said Minako Iida, an economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Iida expects 1997/98 growth to be limited at 1.5 percent.

"There are views within the financial markets that the negative reaction to the tax hike will disappear soon and that the economy will get back on a recovery path by the summer. We want to put a question mark on that," added Salomon's Sakakibara.
